question.prompt:
How many positive integers \(n\) satisfy

\[\frac{n + 1000}{70} = \lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor?\]

(Recall that \(\lfloor x \rfloor\) is the greatest integer not exceeding \(x.\))

solutions.title: Use the floor value as a variable
solutions.explanation:
Using the integer floor value as the variable turns the equation into exact bounds between consecutive squares.

Let \(k=\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor\), a nonnegative integer. The equation gives
\[
n=70k-1000,
\]
and the floor condition is exactly
\[
k^2\le n<(k+1)^2.
\]
Substituting for \(n\) in the lower bound gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
k^2&\le70k-1000,\\
k^2-70k+1000&\le0,\\
(k-35)^2&\le225.
\end{aligned}
\]
Hence \(20\le k\le50\).

The strict upper bound gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
70k-1000&<(k+1)^2,\\
k^2-68k+1001&>0,\\
(k-34)^2&>155.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(k-34\) is an integer and
\[
12^2=144<155<169=13^2,
\]
we must have \(|k-34|\ge13\). Thus \(k\le21\) or \(k\ge47\).

Combining the restrictions yields exactly
\[
k=20,21,47,48,49,50.
\]
Through \(n=70k-1000\), these give
\[
n=400,470,2290,2360,2430,2500.
\]
All are positive and distinct. Since the inequalities used are equivalent to the floor condition, all six satisfy the original equation, and no others can.

The number of solutions is \(\boxed{6}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).

solutions.title: Bound the gap above a square
solutions.explanation:
An integer with floor square root \(k\) lies only a bounded distance above \(k^2\). We can use this gap to eliminate most possibilities before checking a short list.

Let \(k=\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor\) and write
\[
n=k^2+r,
\]
where \(r\) is an integer. The next square is \(k^2+2k+1\), so the floor condition is exactly
\[
0\le r\le2k.
\]
The original equation becomes \(k^2+r+1000=70k\), giving
\[
r=70k-1000-k^2=(k-20)(50-k).
\]
This product is negative outside \(20\le k\le50\), so only that interval is possible. In particular,
\[
r\le2k\le100.
\]

We can exclude the entire interval \(24\le k\le46\). Write \(k=24+u\), where \(0\le u\le22\). Then
\[
r=(4+u)(26-u)=104+u(22-u)\ge104,
\]
contradicting \(r\le100\).

The eight remaining integers can be checked directly using the required gap \(r=(k-20)(50-k)\).

| \(k\) | Required \(r\) | Maximum \(2k\) | Valid? |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| \(20\) | \(0\) | \(40\) | Yes |
| \(21\) | \(29\) | \(42\) | Yes |
| \(22\) | \(56\) | \(44\) | No |
| \(23\) | \(81\) | \(46\) | No |
| \(47\) | \(81\) | \(94\) | Yes |
| \(48\) | \(56\) | \(96\) | Yes |
| \(49\) | \(29\) | \(98\) | Yes |
| \(50\) | \(0\) | \(100\) | Yes |

Exactly six values satisfy the gap condition. Each determines one positive integer \(n=70k-1000\), and different values of \(k\) give different integers \(n\). All other possibilities have been excluded.

Thus there are \(\boxed{6}\) solutions, choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
